records.exact_task: A white beam crosses a glass prism in air and produces a spectrum. Explain why colors separate and predict what turning the prism upside down does.
records.protected_work: Explain color separation and why reversing prism orientation reverses deviation sense.
records.shortest_route: n depends on wavelength; under normal dispersion shorter violet wavelengths have greater deviation toward base. Inverting prism reverses base direction and spatial ordering, not material dispersion.

representation_translation.evidence: Translate prism inversion to base direction and spectrum ordering

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Link dispersion, deviation and orientation change

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Screen order depends on prism orientation

records.misconception: Only if your saved answer demonstrates this error: Thinking prism creates colors absent from monochromatic input. Otherwise record insufficient evidence; compare your actual reasoning with the reconstruction.
records.repair: Separate wavelength composition from wavelength-dependent deviation.
records.boundary: If the refractive index were independent of wavelength, what would white-light output look like?

records.exact_task: For an upright triangular prism in air with horizontal base, draw an incident beam from left, two face normals and a qualitatively correct emerging ray for red and violet under normal dispersion.
records.protected_work: Construct face normals and a geometrically coherent transmitted prism ray.
records.shortest_route: Each face has its own perpendicular normal; both transmitted directions deviate toward base overall; violet is more deviated than red. Actual ray paths are solid.

representation_translation.evidence: Construct two different normals and colored paths preserving order relative to base

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Trace entry/exit for two colors and compare deviations

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Do not use one normal for both faces

records.misconception: Only if your saved answer demonstrates this error: Using one normal for both nonparallel faces or labeling violet by screen side alone. Otherwise record insufficient evidence; compare your actual reasoning with the reconstruction.
records.repair: Draw both normals, track each color along actual directions and label base.
records.boundary: If the prism is replaced by a parallel glass slab, what happens to angular deviation?

records.exact_task: A symmetric ray through a prism A=50° has i=e=40°. Find δ and relative n using Snell at first face.
records.protected_work: Apply prism geometry only in its valid transmission regime.

records.repair: Use r₁+r₂=A; apply Snell at each face and domain check.
records.boundary: If r₂ becomes 50° for n=1.5 to air, does a transmitted angle exist?

records.exact_task: A beam travels through clear air containing tiny particles; viewed from the side it looks blue while transmitted light is warmer. Explain both observations.
records.protected_work: Explain directional color observations using scattering rather than prism dispersion.
records.shortest_route: Short wavelengths scatter more strongly in Rayleigh regime into side directions, depleting them from transmitted beam; direct spectrum shifts toward longer wavelengths.

representation_translation.evidence: Translate side/transmitted observations to wavelength redistribution

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Connect selective scattering to blue side light and depleted transmitted spectrum

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Direction of observation matters

records.misconception: Only if your saved answer demonstrates this error: Assuming every scattering medium produces blue light. Otherwise record insufficient evidence; compare your actual reasoning with the reconstruction.
records.repair: Compare particle size with wavelength and distinguish side-scattered from transmitted light.
records.boundary: What if the incident light is monochromatic red?

records.exact_task: Two chambers contain tiny molecules and large water droplets. Under white illumination, which supports 1/λ⁴ approximation and why?
records.protected_work: Select between Rayleigh approximation, large-particle scattering and refraction from observations.
records.shortest_route: Molecules much smaller than λ support Rayleigh approximation; large droplets do not. Their scattering requires other treatment.

representation_translation.evidence: Translate qualitative size into wavelength comparison

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Compare conditions and choose model

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Large droplets violate Rayleigh

records.misconception: Only if your saved answer demonstrates this error: Using the Rayleigh law for any particles or attributing every color to refraction. Otherwise record insufficient evidence; compare your actual reasoning with the reconstruction.
records.repair: Identify mechanism and particle-size regime before applying a wavelength law.
records.boundary: How could varying particle size change the wavelength dependence?

records.exact_task: Under ideal Rayleigh assumptions compare scattering at 400 and 600 nm; justify whether ratio alone predicts perceived sky color.
records.protected_work: Quantify a conditional scattering ratio and distinguish model limits from observed color.
records.shortest_route: I400/I600=(600/400)^4=5.0625. Perceived color also depends on spectrum, visual sensitivity, path and other effects, so ratio alone insufficient.

representation_translation.evidence: Translate wavelength pair to relative intensity

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Compute ratio then distinguish intensity from perceived color

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Perception depends on more than ratio

records.misconception: Only if your saved answer demonstrates this error: Treating wavelength ratio as intensity ratio or as universal color prediction. Otherwise record insufficient evidence; compare your actual reasoning with the reconstruction.
records.repair: Use fourth-power ratio only in appropriate regime, then state observational limits.
records.boundary: At equal wavelength, what other factors could change scattered intensity?

records.exact_task: A person shifts gaze from a mountain to a nearby book. Explain why greater effective eye power is needed although retina position barely changes.
records.protected_work: Explain accommodation from fixed retinal distance and changing object vergence.
records.shortest_route: Near object sends more divergent rays; to converge at the same retinal plane, effective power must rise. Accommodation increases crystalline lens curvature/power in the simplified model.

representation_translation.evidence: Translate near/distant viewing to incident divergence

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Link changing divergence, increased power and fixed image distance

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Retina not moving to focus

records.misconception: Only if your saved answer demonstrates this error: Assuming focusing occurs mainly by moving the retina. Otherwise record insufficient evidence; compare your actual reasoning with the reconstruction.
records.repair: Compare incoming divergence and required convergence at fixed retinal plane.
records.boundary: How does limited accommodation affect near-point distance?

records.exact_task: An ideal eye has retinal distance 2.5 cm from its effective lens. Find required total power for distant object and object 50 cm away.
records.protected_work: Use a fixed image-plane thin-lens approximation and identify its limits.
records.shortest_route: P∞=1/.025=40 D; P50=1/.025+1/.5=42 D; near viewing requires +2 D accommodation.

concept_model_selection.evidence: Choose fixed-v effective eye lens model

representation_translation.evidence: Translate retinal and object distances into reciprocal power

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Find distant power, near power and difference

algebra_computational_load.evidence: Routine unit conversion and reciprocal arithmetic

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Effective power not full clinical optics

records.misconception: Only if your saved answer demonstrates this error: Changing image distance instead of lens power in the model. Otherwise record insufficient evidence; compare your actual reasoning with the reconstruction.
records.repair: Keep v fixed, use reciprocal object distance in metres.
records.boundary: Does the model describe all aberrations, corneal shape or individual eye anatomy?

records.exact_task: Draw parallel rays for distance vision and diverging rays for near vision entering an effective eye with fixed retina. Show how accommodation changes focus.
records.protected_work: Construct comparative ray diagrams showing focus relative to the retina.
records.shortest_route: Relaxed eye focuses parallel rays on retina. Near rays need more converging power; with same relaxed power they would converge behind retina, increased power brings focus forward onto retina.

representation_translation.evidence: Construct near/distant ray diagrams preserving retinal position and changed convergence

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Draw initial divergence and focal mismatch then corrected convergence

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Retina remains fixed

records.misconception: Only if your saved answer demonstrates this error: Drawing the retina shifting to meet focus. Otherwise record insufficient evidence; compare your actual reasoning with the reconstruction.
records.repair: Mark retina fixed and compare ray convergence for each power.
records.boundary: What happens if the eye cannot increase power enough for close vision?

records.exact_task: A simplified myopic eye has far point 80 cm. Place a thin corrective lens near eye so a distant object's rays match that far-point vergence. Find P.
records.protected_work: Infer correction type and power from stated far/near-point constraint.
records.shortest_route: Object at infinity, required virtual image at −0.80 m, f=−0.80 m, P=−1.25 D; diverging.

concept_model_selection.evidence: Choose corrective lens producing virtual image at far point

representation_translation.evidence: Translate far point to negative virtual image coordinate

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Infer focal length then convert to dioptres and sign

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Correction sign opposite excess eye power

records.misconception: Only if your saved answer demonstrates this error: Giving a myopic eye a converging lens because the image is in front of retina. Otherwise record insufficient evidence; compare your actual reasoning with the reconstruction.
records.repair: Use corrective lens to create the virtual object vergence that the eye can focus.
records.boundary: If glasses sit appreciably away from eye, what distance assumption changes?

records.exact_task: Draw a myopic eye viewing distant rays, then add a corrective diverging lens. Mark far point, pre-correction focus and retinal focus after correction.
records.protected_work: Construct corrective ray paths and show virtual object location without mistaking it for retinal image.
records.shortest_route: Without correction parallel rays converge before retina. Diverger makes rays spread as if from far point on incident side; eye converges them on retina.

concept_model_selection.evidence: Choose diverging correction and eye focusing stages

representation_translation.evidence: Draw two optical transformations with virtual far point and real retinal image

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Trace uncorrected convergence then corrected virtual object and retinal focus

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Correction's virtual image is not retinal image

records.misconception: Only if your saved answer demonstrates this error: Drawing corrective lens as directly forming the final image on retina. Otherwise record insufficient evidence; compare your actual reasoning with the reconstruction.
records.repair: Separate correction's virtual image from subsequent eye focusing.
records.boundary: How would correction differ if the model error were excessive focusing power?

records.exact_task: A learner claims a person with finite far point 2 m needs +0.5 D for distance vision. Justify or reject.
records.protected_work: Check correction sign and feasibility from a quantitative near/far-point model.
records.shortest_route: To view infinity the corrective lens must make a virtual image at −2 m; f=−2 m, P=−0.5 D. Positive power would increase convergence and worsen ideal myopic blur.

representation_translation.evidence: Translate given far point to signed f

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Compute P and reject wrong sign

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Positive correction worsens ideal myopia

records.misconception: Only if your saved answer demonstrates this error: Confusing far-sightedness correction with distance power sign. Otherwise record insufficient evidence; compare your actual reasoning with the reconstruction.
records.repair: Use required virtual-image coordinate and signed lens law.
records.boundary: Can this ideal arithmetic determine an actual eyeglass prescription without eye examination?

records.exact_task: A lens gives a sharp screen image at q=30 cm from object d=60 cm. Find F and percent error if q is called F.
records.protected_work: Infer focal length from measured conjugates and quantify finite-distance approximation error.
records.shortest_route: F=60×30/90=20 cm; q overestimates by 50%.

representation_translation.evidence: Translate screen and object distances to q,d

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Infer F then compute relative error of shortcut

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Finite q overestimates F

records.misconception: Only if your saved answer demonstrates this error: Using q as F for all object distances. Otherwise record insufficient evidence; compare your actual reasoning with the reconstruction.

records.exact_task: A lens bench reports (d,q)=(40,40),(60,30),(80,24) cm. Check consistency with one ideal converging lens.
records.protected_work: Select an experimental model and detect inconsistent measurements.
records.shortest_route: F=20,20,1920/104≈18.46 cm; third inconsistent ignoring uncertainty. Investigate alignment, datum, sharpness or data.

representation_translation.evidence: Translate paired data to focal estimates

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Compute three values then compare with common model

records.exact_task: A pair of converging lenses F=50 cm and 5 cm is available for a simple astronomical telescope. Which should be objective and why? State normal-adjustment separation.
records.protected_work: Select objective and eyepiece roles from object location and desired viewing.
records.shortest_route: Long F objective forms a larger intermediate image for given angular source extent; short F eyepiece yields larger angular magnification. Separation 55 cm; magnitude 10.

concept_model_selection.evidence: Select objective/eyepiece roles in distant-object model

representation_translation.evidence: Translate focal lengths to intermediate image and angular magnification roles

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Choose assignment then calculate normal-adjustment spacing

records.misconception: Only if your saved answer demonstrates this error: Choosing lenses solely because one has larger power or treating microscope object as distant. Otherwise record insufficient evidence; compare your actual reasoning with the reconstruction.

records.protected_work: Connect intermediate image formation and eyepiece placement.
records.shortest_route: Intermediate image 60 cm behind objective, placed at eyepiece front focus 6 cm before it; separation 66 cm. Emergent rays parallel; angular magnitude 10.

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Find intermediate image then spacing and emergent rays

records.exact_task: Sketch a two-converging-lens telescope in normal adjustment for a small off-axis distant source. Mark both foci, intermediate image, eyepiece and outgoing ray bundle.
records.protected_work: Draw two-stage rays preserving intermediate and final image meanings.
records.shortest_route: Incoming parallel tilted bundle forms intermediate image at objective focal plane; this plane coincides with eyepiece front focal plane. Eyepiece produces parallel outgoing bundle at altered angle; inverted angular image.

records.exact_task: Two identical +10 cm lenses image a distant object. Compare ideal contact pair to a pair separated by 5 cm, using sequential model for separated pair.
records.protected_work: Show why fixed total power without separation does not determine final image.
records.shortest_route: Contact F=5 cm. Separated: first would-be focus x=10; second at 5 has u₂=+5; v₂=(1/10+1/5)⁻¹=10/3; final x=25/3≈8.33 cm from first. Different outcome.

records.exact_task: A glass block in air reflects some rays and transmits others at the same exit surface. Explain why total internal reflection occurs only for some incidence angles.
records.protected_work: Explain why both index ordering and angle threshold are necessary.
records.shortest_route: Glass→air higher-to-lower n permits critical angle. Below i_c Snell has propagating r and partial reflection; above i_c no propagating transmitted ray, ideal TIR.

representation_translation.evidence: Translate differing paths at same interface to below/above threshold

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Explain index ordering, critical angle, propagating versus nonpropagating refraction

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Both index ordering and angle threshold required; partial reflection is not TIR

records.misconception: Only if your saved answer demonstrates this error: Assuming high incidence alone guarantees TIR regardless of direction. Otherwise record insufficient evidence; compare your actual reasoning with the reconstruction.
records.repair: Check n_incident>n_transmitted and i>i_c.
records.boundary: At exactly i=i_c, what is the limiting transmitted direction?

records.exact_task: Core n=1.6, cladding n=1.2. A ray strikes boundary at i=55°. Will TIR occur? Then replace cladding with n=1.4.
records.protected_work: Calculate critical-angle admissibility and apply it to a changed surrounding medium.
records.shortest_route: i_c=arcsin(.75)≈48.6°, so yes initially. New i_c=arcsin(.875)≈61.0°, 55° below threshold, no TIR.

concept_model_selection.evidence: Choose critical-angle model with changed cladding

representation_translation.evidence: Translate material change to index ratios and angular comparison

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Compute both thresholds then determine physical regimes

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Change in cladding can reverse transmission regime

records.misconception: Only if your saved answer demonstrates this error: Using sin i_c=n₁/n₂ or comparing angle to surface. Otherwise record insufficient evidence; compare your actual reasoning with the reconstruction.
records.repair: Use n_lower/n_higher and incidence to normal, then test strict inequality.
records.boundary: If cladding index equals core index, can TIR guide rays at the boundary?

records.exact_task: A student says TIR occurs whenever sin i≥n₂/n₁ for any pair of media. Derive and qualify the statement.
records.protected_work: Derive critical boundary and reject incorrect strictness or applicability claims.
records.shortest_route: Snell gives sin r=(n₁/n₂)sin i. Need n₁>n₂ for sub-90° critical. Strict i>i_c gives no propagating transmitted ray; equality is grazing limiting direction. Ideal assumptions matter.

representation_translation.evidence: Translate inequality into critical-angle conditions

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Derive domain, distinguish higher-to-lower and equality versus strict threshold

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Strict inequality and ordering are decisive

records.misconception: Only if your saved answer demonstrates this error: Treating index ordering as sufficient or critical equality as ordinary above-threshold case. Otherwise record insufficient evidence; compare your actual reasoning with the reconstruction.
records.repair: Derive sine domain and compare both conditions.
records.boundary: What changes when the incident side is air and outgoing side glass?
